parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Start by thinking about energy conversion - what type of device is needed to turn an electrical signal into a mechanical sound wave?
Hint 2: Recall the special crystal material used in the probe and the name of the effect where it changes shape when a p.d. is applied.
Hint 3: Consider what kind of electrical supply must be applied to the crystal to make it vibrate continuously, rather than just bend once.
Hint 4: Think about what happens to the amplitude of vibration when the applied frequency equals the natural frequency of the crystal.
Hint 5: Remember the definition of ultrasound in terms of frequency and why short pulses are useful for diagnosis.
parts.proper_answer: A piezoelectric transducer containing a quartz crystal is used. An alternating p.d. applied across the crystal causes it to vibrate with changing shape by the piezoelectric effect. When the frequency of the p.d. equals the natural frequency of the crystal, resonance occurs giving large amplitude oscillations. This produces ultrasound waves of frequency greater than $20\text{ kHz}$. Short pulses are emitted and reflected pulses are detected to form an image.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **The Transducer - Electrical to Mechanical**
You need something that converts electrical energy into sound energy. That is a transducer. In an ultrasound probe this is a piezoelectric crystal, usually quartz.

Step 2: **The Piezoelectric Effect**
This is the key physics. When you apply a p.d. across a piezoelectric crystal it changes shape - it contracts or expands. Reverse the p.d. and it bends the opposite way. So the crystal turns voltage into movement.

Step 3: **Drive It With Alternating Voltage**
If you apply an alternating p.d. of frequency $f$, the crystal is forced to change shape back and forth at that same frequency $f$. It therefore oscillates and emits a sound wave at frequency $f$.

Step 4: **Use Resonance for Large Amplitude**
Like pushing a swing at the right moment, if the frequency of the alternating p.d. is made equal to the natural resonant frequency of the crystal, the crystal resonates. The vibrations build up to a large amplitude, giving an intense ultrasound beam.

Step 5: **Make It Ultrasound and Pulsed**
For medical work the resonant frequency is chosen to be in the ultrasound range, above $20\text{ kHz}$, typically a few MHz. The transducer is driven in short pulses so that emitted pulses and their reflections from boundaries in the body can be observed and timed to build up diagnostic information.

parts.label: (b)
hints: Hint 1: Think about how wave speed $v = f\lambda$ links higher frequency to wavelength, and how wavelength limits the size of detail that can be seen.
parts.proper_answer: Higher frequency gives shorter wavelength, giving greater resolution / more detail of small structures.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Shorter Wavelength Means Finer Detail**
In tissue the speed of ultrasound $c$ is roughly constant, so from $$c = f\lambda$$ a higher $f$ means a smaller $\lambda$. A wave cannot resolve detail much smaller than its own wavelength because of diffraction. So a 10 MHz wave has a very short wavelength and can distinguish very small or closely spaced structures, giving a sharper, more detailed image.
